1:
The chapter opens with a command and no verb. Keil and Delitzsch notes that the first sentence is an exclamation, the summons issuing from Jehovah to the prophet, who is to blow the trumpet as God's herald; he sets the whole in three strophes, an enumeration of Israel's sins, a reference to the fall already beginning, and a warning against false security. Gill gives the Hebrew as the trumpet to the roof of thy mouth, a concise expression denoting haste and vehemence. Calvin calls it an exhibition, since God clothes his prophets with various characters, and makes this one a herald proclaiming war, commanded not to speak but to show by the trumpet that war was near. Henry has him do the part of a watchman calling the besieged to arms, and Clarke hears the alarm in the style, the chapter beginning in short broken sentences expressive of sudden danger.

Whose house is threatened divides them. Calvin reports that interpreters nearly all take the house of God for the temple and refer the opening to Judah; he dissents, wondering they should have mistaken so trifling a matter, since the house of God means not the temple only but the whole people, and Israel had retained exactly that boast, that they were a holy people and God's own family. Had anything been added that belonged peculiarly to Judah he would accede, but the context lays down no difference, and Israel is named in the next verse while the discourse runs on unbroken. Wesley agrees in a line: the house of the Lord is the family of Israel. Ellicott makes the same identification with an edge, that Hosea gives Samaria the name House of Jehovah with some irony, since the calf had been meant as in some sense a symbol of Israel's God. Henry allows both readings: on the one the eagle is a named invader coming against the temple, on the other the body of the people, to whom pertained the adoption and the covenants, is called the house of the Lord; they thought that title would protect them, but having lost the life of their religion while keeping its form they were only a carcase for the eagles. Ellicott and Wesley agree that the eagle stands for swiftness, Wesley adding hunger and the surmounting of all difficulties.

On the charge Henry distinguishes two counts: every sin transgresses the command, but these transgressed the covenant, breaking the original contract, which is in effect to declare they will be God's people no longer. He traces the decline: men first cast off what is good, omissions make way for commissions, and repeated transgression brings men at last to a habitual renunciation of the covenant.

The cry of the next verse is taken by all as hypocrisy, though its grammar is not settled. Gill has them crying in distress as they always did when troubled, pretending acquaintance after hundreds of years of serving idols; he notes that Israel stands last in the verse and has produced different renderings, either we Israel know thee or we know thee who are Israel. Ellicott would render it to me they cry, My God, we know thee, we Israel. Calvin sets aside two other constructions, that the people are blamed for not fleeing to God and that the words are an exhortation to cry now, and takes them as they stand: they cherished wickedness while pretending God's name even in prayer, and though hypocrites affirm with a lofty air that they are God's people, God laughs the boasting to scorn. Keil and Delitzsch states the principle, that a knowledge of God which is no more than historical acquaintance cannot bring salvation, and Clarke finds the same words in the Gospel, where those who claim to have prophesied in the name are told they were never known. Wesley reduces it to four words: they cry, but not sincerely.
3:
What was cast off is read three ways. Gill takes the good for God himself, the chiefest good and fountain of all goodness, rejected with the detestation the word implies by a people who pretended to know him; and he reports a bolder rendering in which subject and object change places, so that the good One has cast off Israel, noting that some have preferred it as suiting what follows but that the Hebrew order and the accents do not favour it. Ellicott agrees that the good is the name of God, which is the salvation of Israel, and adds a note on the verb, that it means a scornful loathing of what is putrescent. Calvin dissents from both. He doubts the word is masculine and refers to God, and takes the prophet to accuse Israel simply of having driven far off everything right and just. On his reading the verse turns on a contrast: they repelled good and the enemy pursues them, so that there is no better defence against harm than attention to piety, and a people from whom integrity is banished lie open to every evil for want of God's aid.

The charge about kings raises a difficulty every voice feels. Gill locates the right where it belongs: the people had no title to choose a king, the choosing being the Lord's alone as it had been for the first three kings; and it was not the person of the first northern king that God disliked but their taking the appointment on themselves, several of his successors being conspirators who set themselves up over the slaughter of others. Wesley names four of them. Clarke states the consequence flatly, that properly not one of the kings of that line from the defection onward was the anointed of the Lord, and glosses the clause I knew it not to mean that the thing had not his approbation, a sense the word often carries. Keil and Delitzsch refers the charge chiefly to the founding of the kingdom but declines to restrict it there, extending it to their obstinate persistence at every later usurpation, and notes the awkward fact on the other side, that a prophet had foretold the first king's rule and a later king was anointed at a prophet's command. Ellicott meets that by dividing the history: the revolt of the ten tribes did receive divine sanction, though it ran against the idea that associated true religion with the line of David, and this passage is best referred to the short reigns of usurpers and the murders that disgraced the annals afterwards, from which God repudiates all participation.

Calvin thinks interpreters have not considered the design closely enough. The salvation of that people was founded on a kingdom and a priesthood, by which God testified that he was allied to the children of Abraham, since in the priesthood shone the image of the Mediator and in the person of David the kingdom of Christ. When they tumultuously chose a new king without any command, built a new temple and altar against what the law prescribed, and divided the priesthood, they undermined the whole appointment of God and showed they were unwilling to be ruled by his hand; they would never have dared depart from the house of David, Calvin says, had any particle of the fear of God prevailed in their hearts. That is why he sets the two clauses of the verse side by side, the new kingdom and the made idols, as one apostasy in two directions. Ellicott adds a small correction to the second half, that the words should read knew them not, meaning the gold and silver splendours with which Israel had adorned its apostasy. Clarke reads the closing purpose clause as consequence rather than intention, that they shall be cut off in consequence of their idolatry.
5:
The opening clause is rendered four ways. Gill offers three himself: that the calf is the cause of Samaria being cast off, the past tense standing for the future as often in prophecy; or that the calf has left thee in the lurch and cannot help; or that the enemy has removed thy calf, since when the king of Assyria took the city he seized it for the sake of its gold. Calvin thinks the probable sense is that the calf drove Samaria far off, and presses his usual point, that the coming captivity would not happen by chance nor be ascribable to enemies, since the cause was to be sought nowhere but in their own wickedness. Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott take the verb intransitively: the calf is loathsome, it disgusts, and Keil and Delitzsch ties the word back to the earlier verse, so that as Israel felt disgust at what was good, so does the Lord at this. Ellicott says nothing can exceed the scorn of it. Clarke reports yet another rendering, in which the clause is a command, remove far from thee thy calf, and abandon thy idolatry.

Where the calf stood is also disputed. Gill explains the name from the capital, the calf being called the calf of Samaria because that was the metropolis. Keil and Delitzsch denies a calf ever stood in the city itself, since history mentions none, and takes Samaria for the kingdom, the calf meant being the one at Bethel. On the closing question the voices agree in substance: Ellicott would render it how long are ye unable to attain purity, Keil and Delitzsch how long are they incapable of it, Clarke how long will ye continue these guilty practices, and Wesley how long will it be before they repent and reform.

Where the calf came from is the burden of the next verse. Gill sets out several possibilities, that it was Israel's own contrivance rather than a borrowing, or that it was made by the advice of their king and princes, or that the metal was exacted from them; and he draws a distinction, that the making of the image was their own but the worship of it came from Egypt, with this difference, that there a living beast was worshipped and here the golden likeness of one. Wesley says simply that it was of their own invention. Calvin finds an implied comparison in the word also and gives it great weight: the calf is from Israel as the calf in the desert had been from Israel, so that they are now the second time the fabricators of this superstition. Their fathers could not plead that the offence was presented to them by the nations and that they were ensnared as men often are; they founded a new superstition through their own inclination, and so here the evil has been generated within. Ellicott would abandon the received punctuation and translate that the calf is from Israel and not of divine origin, an artificer made it and it is no god.

Clarke turns the same clause into an argument. Since God means the supreme eternal Good, the Creator and upholder of all things, the workman cannot have made him who made all things; the workman has made them, therefore they are not God, and he thinks nothing need be added to that. He also traces the pedigree of the worship, that the ox was a supreme deity in Egypt and it was there the people learned this, a white ox worshipped under one name at one city and another elsewhere; and he remarks that the superstition is among the most ancient and still prevails in the East, the cow being sacred among the Hindoos.
7:
The proverb is expounded by every voice, and pulled two ways. Gill and Wesley read the sowing as wasted labour: the people took great pains in their worship and made a great noise, promising themselves peace and plenty, and got nothing by it but what was worse than nothing, since God's wrath and an invading army would rush on them like a storm. Clarke turns it into arithmetic, that as the husbandman reaps the grain he sowed but thirty or sixty or a hundredfold, so a man who sows wind reaps a whirlwind, the seed multiplied into a tempest; he calls it a fine and energetic metaphor. Calvin reads the sowing as pretence rather than labour. To sow the wind is to put on an appearance that dazzles the simple and covers impiety with a guise of words, so that a man seems to cast seed and casts nothing; hypocrites set themselves in order until they look wholly like true worshippers, and their sacrifices conformed to the law, but there was no faith in the service and so it was wind. Ellicott finds in it a law of retribution, that the punishment of sin is often a greater facility in sinning, indifference becoming enmity and forgetfulness of duty a violent recoil from it.

The failure of the crop is traced through its stages. Clarke follows them one by one: nothing can yield a blossom; if there is a blossom it will not yield fruit; if there is fruit the sower will not enjoy it, since strangers shall eat it. Wesley says the same of dependence on idols and foreign help, that it is seed bearing neither stalk nor bud, and that any bud will be blasted before it yields meal. Ellicott hears a play of words in the Hebrew, that the growth shall yield no grain, and takes the clause to deny them even the incipient prosperity of an earlier reign.

The swallowing that follows is read as already begun. Gill says it takes in not only their substance but their persons, the whole nation, the present tense standing for the future because the thing is certain. Keil and Delitzsch locates the advance of the threat in the tense itself, a perfect indicating that the evil seed has already ripened, so that they have become among the nations like a despised vessel men throw away, a lot they prepared for themselves. Calvin notices that the same verb was used of the meal a moment before, and says that not the provision only but the people are devoured; the prophet's object was to make them feel their evils and learn to pray for pardon, since it is great wisdom to profit so far under God's scourges that our sins come before our eyes. He measures the fall by the height: a people chosen as peculiar and set apart from the nations is now dispersed and everywhere despised, which could not have happened unless God had withdrawn his protection.

The vessel is described variously. Ellicott calls it worthless, devoted to the vilest uses or smashed up. Clarke thinks of a skin-bottle of goat or calf hide such as is still used in Asia and Africa, and contrasts a handsome one, dressed and painted and hung with fringes, with the old and musty sort to which Israel is compared. Henry stays with the disgrace: impoverished, they have lost their credit like a merchant gone bankrupt, so that no neighbour cares to have anything to do with them; and he draws the rule, that those who have professed religion and then degenerate are of all men the most contemptible, since salt that has lost its savour is fit only to be trodden under foot. He allows also that the phrase may denote their dispersion, poor and prisoners among the nations, and asks who has pleasure in such.
9:
Going up to Assyria is read as diplomacy, not deportation. Gill says so expressly, that this is not the captivity but an embassy to gain the king's friendship, as a king of Israel once did who went out to meet an invader and paid a thousand talents of silver to make him a confederate; and yet, he adds, this did not hinder Israel from being swallowed up by that same people at last. Ellicott notices the choice of verb, since the word rendered going up is elsewhere used of going up to the sanctuary of the Lord. Calvin makes the journey itself the charge: they ought not to have hastened to Assyria as though destitute of help, knowing themselves protected by the hand of God, and in reckoning as nothing the help he stood ready to give they showed plain ingratitude.

The wild ass is described from several sides. Wesley calls it stubborn and untamed and alone where there is no path, which he applies to their state in captivity. Calvin hears in it the brutish wildness of a people that can by no means be tamed, and notes that another prophet uses the same similitude. Keil and Delitzsch turns the comparison the other way and warns against supplying a word of likeness: the point is not that Israel is like a wild ass, but that even a wild ass, stupid as it is, keeps to itself, whereas Israel went suing for loves. Ellicott describes the animal from a traveller's account, dirty yellow, long-eared, with a head like a gazelle's and a pace no huntsman can overtake, and observes that it is seldom seen alone but in herds, though another prophet shows it wandering alone after the object of its lust; so Israel courts strange alliances. Clarke reports from an ancient naturalist that a single male keeps a whole flock of females and suffers no rival, and applies that jealousy of liberty to a people who took no step that did not lead to their own thraldom. On the last clause Clarke says they subsidised the neighbouring states, and Ellicott that Ephraim pays abnormally for her own shame.

The gathering in the next verse is the hardest clause here, and every voice handles it differently. Wesley reads it as assembling them together so that they may be taken and destroyed together. Calvin reports the received explanation, that God would gather the hired nations against Israel, and prefers to refer the word to the people themselves; even so he allows two senses, either that the forces they had gathered would not prevent God from throwing them into a heap by slaughter, or that Israel, running among the nations in a heat that is itself dispersion, would be gathered against its own will and preserved for a time. Ellicott says much depends on whom the pronoun means, prefers Ephraim to the nations, and renders it that God will gather them in restraint so that they cannot roam seeking help, with the result that in a short time they will delay to render the tribute; he notes that such non-payment did occur a few years later, and reports the rival rendering in which God gathers the nations to look scornfully on her ruin and they sorrow a little, the phrase used ironically. Calvin sets out a further ambiguity in the verb, derived by some from a root meaning to begin, so that they begin to be burdened, and by others from a root meaning to grieve, so that they sorrow a little for the burden. Clarke identifies that burden as the exactions of the Assyrian king and the princes of the provinces, and Wesley as the tribute laid on them, sorrowed over for a while before the final captivity. Gill points out who else was courted, since the Egyptians were privately engaged to help shake off the Assyrian yoke and its yearly presents.
11:
The paradox of altars built to sin is unfolded carefully. Gill guards the intention: the altars were not raised to commit sin but to offer sacrifice for it, as the builders supposed; yet being erected for idols they were themselves sin, and the cause of sin in others drawn in by the example, as the people had first been drawn in by their king. He locates them at the two famous shrines and in the high places, against the command that required sacrifice at one place and on one altar, which he takes as typical of the one sacrifice of Christ, so that those who use more, or neglect him, fall into the same fault. Ellicott makes the legal point, that multiplication of altars was condemned in the law and that unity of altar and sanctuary was essential to the unity of the nation; he would render the last clause he had altars for sinning, and notes that the word means transgression in the first half and transgression with its guilt in the second. Calvin explains how such a thing becomes invisible to those doing it: where error has once prevailed it gains firmness by length of time, and these men thought they did the most meritorious of deeds whenever they sacrificed, so that it was hard to persuade them that the more attentive they were in worship the more grievously they offended.

Clarke and Wesley read the second half of the verse quite differently, of altars not yet built. On their view, because they made many altars to sin at home they were compelled in the land of their captivity to keep up a similar idolatry against their will, so that they felt the evil of it without power to help themselves; Wesley says plainly that the altars meant are those they shall find in Assyria, the occasion of greater guilt and punishment. Henry states the principle covering both readings, that it is a great sin to corrupt the worship of God and will be charged as sin on all who do it, however plausible their excuses; offerings of men's own devising, however costly, are to them for sin, since only those services are acceptable which are done according to God's word.

The written law is described by its fullness. Gill takes it for the whole body given through Moses, a multiplicity of commands moral and ceremonial, and particularly those concerning sacrifices, which showed what they should be and on what altar offered, and pointed forward to the Messiah, who is altar and sacrifice and priest at once; and the prophets sent from time to time were continually writing the same things again, so that ignorance could not be pleaded. Wesley says the same in a line, written by Moses first and by other prophets afterwards. Clarke renders the clause as an inscription, that God had as it were inscribed his laws to them and they treated them as matters in which they had no interest, and Henry that they cared not to know them and would not obey.

Calvin uses the verse to settle the question of worship. The prophet sets the law and the rule it prescribes against all the inventions of men, who think God unjust unless he accepts whatever they have imagined; but obedience, as another Scripture says, is preferred by him to all sacrifices. Hence there is no need of many words in contending with the superstitious, however daringly they devise kinds of worship wholly different from what God commands: they are to be pressed with this one thing, that a certain rule is contained in the law, and that departing from it is not zeal but disobedience.
13:
The opening clause is obscure and is rendered three ways. Clarke reports a version that reads they sacrifice gifts appointed unto me and eat flesh, and offers two senses of it, either that they give to idols the things belonging to the Lord, or that while pretending to offer to him they eat and drink idolatrously. Ellicott would render it they sacrifice the sacrifices of my gifts, flesh, and eat it, and calls the phrase a clear reference to the Mosaic institute. Calvin reports that interpreters generally think the Israelites are derided for trusting their ceremonies, the sacrifices being contemptuously called flesh, but suspects something deeper. He canvasses the derivations of the disputed word, some taking it for offerings burnt or roasted and others from a root meaning to give gifts, which he says is the more received opinion; and he prefers a reading that makes the contempt palpable enough for a child to condemn. Where burnt-offerings were owed, flesh is what they bring: fearing lest any portion be lost, they keep entire what they ought to have burned, turning a burnt-offering into a peace-offering so that the meat may remain for eating. It has always been a dominant vice in hypocrites, Calvin adds, to connect gain with superstition, and however devoted idolaters may show themselves they take care that nothing goes to waste.

The return to Egypt is read as fact and as figure together. Clarke says many did return there after the conquest of the land, and many again after the later ruin of Jerusalem, but adds that they had in effect returned already by setting up golden calves in imitation of the Egyptian bull. Wesley makes it flight, that many shall fly from the Assyrian into Egypt. Ellicott allows both, either the positive return or the disastrous hankering after Egyptian alliances, and hears in the threat that they shall go back and there learn again the bitter lessons of the past.

On forgetting the Maker Gill dwells on what was forgotten: the Creator and Preserver of every one of them, who had raised them into a state and kingdom and made them great and rich and populous, and had bestowed so many favours, and was yet not served nor given glory. Clarke sets the two halves of the verse in parallel, that Israel forgot his Maker and therefore built temples to other gods, while Judah had lost all confidence in the divine protection and therefore built many fenced cities, and that the fire of God's anger burnt up both alike. Wesley says the temples are idol temples, and dates the devouring of the palaces to the day when the cities of both kingdoms were laid in ashes.

Ellicott adds the archaeology. The word used here for temple is used sixty times of the Lord's own temple, so that building these temple-palaces was a distinct sin against the unity of the Godhead; and the fortified cities of the southern kingdom, erected by two named kings, are referred to in an Assyrian inscription whose author boasts of besieging and capturing forty-six of them. Calvin closes on the paradox in the word forgotten. Israel might have objected that nothing of the kind was intended, and that the temples were built precisely in order to retain the remembrance of God; but the prophet shows that God is not truly known, and men do not really remember him, except when they worship according to what the law prescribes and attempt nothing but what he has commanded. What the superstitious call remembrance, Calvin says, the prophet here plainly testifies is forgetfulness. He notes also that this verse concludes the foregoing teaching, and that the prophet, who preached these things daily and often repeated the same threatenings, afterwards collected the heads of his sermons into chapters so that we might know what his teaching was.
